pos: n. (Daniel Toussain, 1541–1602, Huguenot pastor and professor at Heidelberg)
etymology: Hebrew Daniel, God is my judge; French Toussain, from Toussaint, All Saints, Latinized Tossanus.
biblical_def: Daniel Tossanus was pastor at Orleans when the massacre of St Bartholomew came in 1572, and he lost his church, his library and very nearly his life in the months that followed. He fled east, served the scattered French congregations of the Rhineland, and ended his days as professor of theology and court preacher at Heidelberg, where he had charge of the French-speaking refugees whom the Palatinate took in. He is the type of a whole generation: men who did not choose a professor's chair but were driven into one, and who carried into the lecture hall the memory of a congregation butchered in the street. The Palatinate itself changed religion three times in his lifetime, Reformed under Frederick III, Lutheran under Lewis VI, Reformed again under John Casimir, and Tossanus was turned out of Heidelberg once and brought back. A man so moved learns to hold his comfort somewhere other than in his settlement, and the lesson is the one Jeremiah sent to the captives: pray for the peace of the city you did not choose (Jer 29:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refugee as one who flees to a place of safety, and exile as the state of being banished from one's country.
webster_full: REF'UGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; particularly, one who flees from his country to escape persecution.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being expelled from one's native country; banishment.
PRO'FESSOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university.
MAS'SACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty.
scriptures: Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
corruption_summary: A pastor turned out of two countries, who taught that a man's rest is not in his settlement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of treating displacement as the defining fact about a man, so that the refugee becomes a category of victimhood rather than a person under the hand of God. Tossanus was genuinely robbed, and Scripture never pretends that such robbery is nothing; but the Authorized Version does not permit a sufferer to be reduced to his suffering. Jeremiah's letter to the captives of Babylon commands them to build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the city that had taken them, which is a commission, not a consolation prize.

The principle to recover is that providence appoints the place as well as the work, and that the man who has lost his place has not lost his Master. “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it” (Jer 29:7). Paul puts the same settledness in its final form: “whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8).

pos: n. (Jeremias Bastingius, 1551–1595, Dutch minister and expositor of the Heidelberg Catechism)
etymology: Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the LORD exalts, Latinized Jeremias; Dutch surname Latinized Bastingius.
biblical_def: Jeremias Bastingius gave the Heidelberg Catechism its first great commentary. He had studied at Heidelberg and Geneva, served Dutch congregations at Antwerp and Dordrecht, and ended as a curator of the university of Leiden; but his lasting work is the exposition in which every question of the Catechism is opened, defended from Scripture, and turned to use. It was printed in Latin in 1588, translated into English the following year, and for a generation it was bound up at the back of Scottish and English Bibles, so that a ploughman in Ayrshire who had never heard of the Palatinate was being catechized by Heidelberg. That is the quiet way doctrine travels: not by proclamation but by a printed page carried in the same volume as the text it expounds. Luke tells Theophilus exactly why such a book exists, that thou mightest know the certainty of those things (Luk 1:4). A catechism asks the question; an exposition gives the sense, which is what the Levites did when the law was read at the water gate (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exposition as explanation, and catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer.
webster_full: EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author, or of any writing.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CERTAIN'TY, n. A full assurance of mind; exemption from doubt.
COMMENT'ARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; a book of explanations.
INSTRUCT'ED, pp. Taught; educated; directed; informed.

That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
Neh 8:8

corruption_summary: The Catechism's first expositor, bound at the back of English Bibles for a generation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of the catechism itself, treated as rote imposition on a child who ought rather to construct his own convictions. The objection mistakes what a catechism is. It is not a substitute for conviction; it is the furnishing of a mind with the words in which conviction can be held, and Bastingius wrote six hundred pages to show that every one of those words answers to a text.

The principle to recover is that instruction aims at certainty, not at the perpetual suspension of judgment. “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). The method is as old as Nehemiah: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). And the charge runs down the generations: “but teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons” (Deu 4:9).

pos: n. (Heinrich Alting, 1583–1644, professor at Heidelberg and Groningen, delegate to Dort)
etymology: German Heinrich, from Old High German Heimerich, ruler of the house; Alting, a Frisian family name.
biblical_def: Heinrich Alting taught theology at Heidelberg through the years in which the Palatinate was ruined. He had been tutor to the young Frederick V, the elector whose acceptance of the Bohemian crown brought the imperial armies down on his own country; he sat at the Synod of Dort as one of the Palatinate delegates; and in 1622 he watched Tilly's troops take Heidelberg, the great library carried off to Rome, and the university closed. He escaped, taught the scattered Palatine students where he could, and at length took a chair at Groningen, where he wrote the historical theology that is his monument. His life answers a question the comfortable seldom ask: what is a professor for, when the university is gone? The answer he gave was to keep teaching the men who were left, and to write down for a later generation what this one had been taught (Psa 102:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines library as a collection of books, and synod as an ecclesiastical council.
webster_full: LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
DEL'EGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
STEW'ARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and keep the accounts.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Jer 29:7

Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Heidelberg's library went to Rome; the teaching went to Groningen in a man's head.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of a school with its buildings and its endowment, so that the loss of the one is read as the end of the other. The Palatine library was the finest in Germany and its loss was a real calamity; but the deposit is not a building. Paul does not tell Timothy to preserve an institution. He tells him to commit what he has heard to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also, and that transmission survived the sack of Heidelberg.

The principle to recover is that the written record of a generation's faith is itself an act of stewardship toward a generation not yet born. “This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD” (Psa 102:18). And the trust is measured by one standard only: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

pos: n. (Jacobus Kimedoncius, c. 1550–1596, professor of theology at Heidelberg)
etymology: Hebrew Yaakov, he takes by the heel, Latinized Jacobus; Kimedoncius, a Latinized Netherlandish surname.
biblical_def: Jacobus Kimedoncius wrote the book the English Reformed needed before they had Owen. His treatise on the redemption of mankind, printed in Latin in 1592 and in English in 1598, took up the question whether Christ died for all men without exception and answered it from the texts rather than from the temper of the age. He taught at Heidelberg in the years between Ursinus and the Synod of Dort, and his work is one of the bridges between the Catechism and the Canons: the definite, effectual, particular purpose of the atonement set out with care a generation before the Remonstrants forced the whole church to speak. He is almost unread now, which is a loss, because the argument he makes is not a deduction from a system but an exposition of what the Scriptures say Christ came to do. The rule he worked by is the prophet's rule: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them (Isa 8:20).

ATONE'MENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.

TREA'TISE, n. A tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed.

corruption_summary: A Heidelberg defence of definite redemption, printed in English six years before Dort was called.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is older and more respectable: the claim that definite atonement is a late scholastic hardening, invented at Dort or by the English Puritans, and absent from the first Reformers. Kimedoncius is one of the plain refutations of that claim. He was writing in the 1590s, before the Remonstrance existed, and he was not innovating but gathering what Heidelberg already held.

The principle to recover is that a doctrine is tried by Scripture and not by its date. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). An elder's qualification is the ability to do exactly this work: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

pos: n. (Pierre Boquin, c. 1518–1582, first Reformed professor of theology at Heidelberg)
etymology: Greek Petros, a stone, Latinized Petrus; French Boquin, Latinized Boquinus.
biblical_def: Petrus Boquinus was a French Carmelite who read the Reformers, left his order, and spent the rest of his life teaching the doctrine he had come to believe. He taught at Bourges, at Strasbourg, and from 1557 at Heidelberg, where he held the chair of theology before Ursinus arrived and worked with him afterward in framing the Palatinate's Reformed settlement. He stood with Ursinus against the Lutheran party in the long quarrel over the Lord's Supper, and when the elector Lewis VI turned the Palatinate Lutheran again Boquinus was dismissed and went to Lausanne to die. He planted where another watered; the increase was not his to give (1Co 3:6). The dictionary notes him chiefly because the men who begin a work are so often remembered less than the men who finish it, and Scripture is careful about that: the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and the keeping is the office, whoever gets the credit (Mal 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plant as to set in the earth for growth, and increase as augmentation, growth, that which is added.
webster_full: PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the earth for propagation.
IN'CREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; extension; that which is added.

corruption_summary: Heidelberg's first Reformed theologian, dismissed by the next elector and remembered by few.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern appetite for the founder and the headline, which leaves the second man and the groundbreaker unnamed. Boquinus held the Heidelberg chair before the Catechism was written, prepared the ground that Ursinus and Olevianus built on, and was turned out by a prince who changed his mind. He has no monument and needs none.

The principle to recover is that God divides the labour and keeps the increase in His own hand. “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6). The work itself is defined without reference to reputation: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7). Ezra shows the order in which a teacher is made: “Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel” (Ezr 7:10).

pos: n. (Georg Sohn, 1551–1589, professor of theology at Heidelberg)
etymology: Greek Georgios, a husbandman, a tiller of the soil; German Sohn, a son.
biblical_def: Georg Sohn was a Hessian who taught first at Marburg and then at Heidelberg, where he spent the last years of his short life answering Rome. His method was the one the Reformed polemicists made their own: take the Roman writer's own words, set them beside the text of Scripture, and let the distance between the two make the argument. He died at thirty-eight with much of his work unfinished, and his collected writings were published after his death by colleagues who thought the answers worth keeping. The dictionary honours him as one of a company of men whose whole public labour was controversy, a vocation modern Christians are taught to regard as a failure of charity. Jude calls it a duty laid on the beloved (Jud 1:3), and Paul makes the ability to convince the gainsayers a qualification for office, not a defect of temper (Tit 1:9).

webster_full: POLEM'IC, a. Controversial; disputative; intended to maintain an opinion or system in opposition to others.
GAINSA'Y, v.t. To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.
CONTROVER'SY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
CONVINCE', v.t. To persuade or satisfy the mind by evidence; to subdue the opposition of the mind to truth.

corruption_summary: Thirty-eight years, most of them spent answering Rome from the text.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentiment that doctrinal controversy is in itself unspiritual, so that a man who spends his life in dispute has wasted it however right he was. That sentiment is not in Scripture. Sohn disputed because Rome was teaching men to look for righteousness where it is not, and a shepherd who watches that happen in silence is not gentle but faithless.

The principle to recover is that contending for the faith is commanded, and that the test of a controversialist is whether he argues from the word or from himself. “Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The watch is double, and the order matters: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16).

pos: n. (Quirinus Reuter, 1558–1613, professor at Heidelberg and editor of Ursinus)
etymology: Latin Quirinus, an old Roman divine name; German Reuter, a rider, a horseman.
biblical_def: Quirinus Reuter studied under Zacharias Ursinus, taught at Heidelberg for the rest of his life, and did the work without which a teacher's labour dies with him: he gathered his master's lectures, papers and letters and published them. The collected works of Ursinus exist because Reuter spent years on other men's manuscripts instead of his own. He was also one of the Heidelberg men who held the Reformed line through the Palatinate's second restoration, and he taught the students who would sit for the Palatinate at Dort. His life is an argument for a kind of service the church never ranks highly and cannot do without: the editor, the copyist, the man who makes a dead teacher audible. Paul describes the chain and leaves the editor's part implied: the things thou hast heard of me, commit thou to faithful men (2Ti 2:2).

MAN'USCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing of any kind in distinction from print.

corruption_summary: He published his master's works instead of his own, and so Ursinus still speaks.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of a scholar by his own output, which quietly writes the editor, the translator and the copyist out of the account. Reuter's own books are few. The Ursinus that later generations read is the Ursinus he assembled, and a great deal of the Reformation survives in exactly that way, through men who preferred another man's voice to their own.

The principle to recover is that the deposit is something handed on, and that handing on is itself a form of sound teaching. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). The commission runs four deep in one verse: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Solomon describes what the printed lectures became: “as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd” (Ecc 12:11).

pos: n. (Johann Jacob Grynaeus, 1540–1617, antistes of Basel)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, Latinized Johannes; Grynaeus, a Hellenized family name.
biblical_def: Johann Jacob Grynaeus was born a Lutheran, became Reformed by study, taught briefly at Heidelberg in the Palatinate's Reformed restoration, and then served Basel as its chief pastor for thirty years. Under him Basel moved decisively into the Reformed camp, subscribed with the Swiss churches, and became a refuge for Huguenot and English exiles. He corresponded across Europe, catechized, and kept a city church ordered through decades of war to the north. His career shows what the Reformation looked like when it was not a battle but a maintenance: the same doctrine preached in the same pulpit for a generation, the young instructed, the refugees housed, the magistrates reminded of their duty. Aquila and Priscilla did the same thing in a private house, and the whole church is still living on the effect of it (Act 18:26).

webster_full: PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation, whose duty is to watch over the people of his charge.

corruption_summary: Thirty years in one Basel pulpit, and a city that came over to the Reformed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the Reformation was carried by dramatic conversions and public confrontations, which makes the long steady ministry look like an anticlimax. Basel did not change by a crisis. It changed because a man preached the same doctrine for thirty years, taught the children, received the refugees, and outlasted the opposition.

The principle to recover is that teaching is ordinarily patient, private and cumulative. “And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26). The office is defined by what the mouth keeps: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7). And instruction compounds in a teachable man: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (Bartholomaeus Keckermann, c. 1572–1609, Reformed logician of Danzig and Heidelberg)
etymology: Aramaic Bar-Talmai, son of Talmai, Latinized Bartholomaeus; German Keckermann, a family name.
biblical_def: Bartholomew Keckermann was the great Reformed methodist of his generation, in the old sense of that word: a man preoccupied with how a body of knowledge should be ordered so that it can be taught. Born at Danzig, trained at Heidelberg, he lectured there in Hebrew and philosophy before returning home to teach at the Danzig gymnasium, and he produced systems of logic, rhetoric, ethics, politics and theology, each arranged so that a student could see the whole before he learned the parts. He died at thirty-seven. His work shaped the textbooks of Reformed schools for a century and drew the criticism that always follows such labour, that he had made divinity into a science. The charge is worth weighing, and Scripture supplies the warning in its own terms: beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy (Col 2:8). Order serves the text or it supplants it, and there is no third possibility.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines method as a suitable and convenient arrangement of things, and logic as the art of reasoning.
webster_full: METH'OD, n. A suitable and convenient arrangement of things, proceedings or ideas; the natural or regular disposition of separate parts.
LOG'IC, n. The art of thinking and reasoning justly; the art of using reason well in our inquiries after truth.
SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a whole plan or scheme.
PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the phenomena or effects of nature, and of the causes which produce them.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: Thirty-seven years, and textbooks that ordered Reformed schooling for a century.
corruption_paragraphs: A real danger attends this kind of work and the dictionary names it rather than excusing it. When a system is built well, the system begins to be taught instead of the Scripture it was built to serve, and the student learns the arrangement so thoroughly that he can no longer be surprised by the text. Paul is not warning against thinking; he is warning against a frame imported from outside and then laid over Christ. “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8).

The principle to recover is that order is a servant. A method that drives students into the text is a goad and a nail; a method that lets them stop short of the text is a cage. “The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd” (Ecc 12:11). And the disputer of this world is given his place at the beginning of the inquiry, not at the end: “hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20).

pos: n. (Friedrich Spanheim the Elder, 1600–1649, professor at Geneva and Leiden)
etymology: German Friedrich, peace-ruler; Spanheim, from the Rhenish place-name Sponheim.
biblical_def: Friedrich Spanheim the Elder was a son of the Palatinate who had to make his life elsewhere. Born at Amberg and educated at Heidelberg, he was driven out with the rest when the imperial armies came, taught at Geneva for sixteen years, and finished at Leiden. He wrote against the Arminians and against Rome, defended the Reformed account of grace with a thoroughness that wearied his opponents, and raised a son who would do the same work in the next generation. What marks him is the absence of self-pity in a career entirely shaped by other men's wars. He believed what he taught about providence, which is the only reason a man in his position can keep writing at all. Paul had the same ground under him when he quoted the psalm: I believed, and therefore have I spoken (2Co 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines defend as to maintain or vindicate, and conversation as general course of manners, behaviour, deportment.
webster_full: DEFEND', v.t. To maintain or vindicate; to uphold or support against attack; to repel an accusation.
CONVERSA'TION, n. General course of manners; behavior; deportment; especially as it respects morals.
STRIVE, v.i. To make efforts; to use exertions; to endeavor with earnestness; to labor hard.
BAN'ISHMENT, n. The act of compelling a citizen to leave his country; the state of being banished; exile.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak;
Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
corruption_summary: Driven out of the Palatinate, he spent thirty years defending the doctrine it had taught him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern expectation that a man displaced by war will write about his displacement, and the corresponding suspicion of a man who instead writes doctrine. Spanheim lost his country at twenty-two and produced volumes on grace and on the Roman controversy. That is not avoidance. It is a judgment about what will still matter when the armies have gone home.

The principle to recover is that faith speaks, and that what it speaks is not chiefly its own story. “We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak” (2Co 4:13). The exile's prayer is for the work, not for the restoration of the place: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17). And the standing is corporate: “with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel” (Php 1:27).
